8.	Reverend Kotowski is a doctor in political and social sciences. 1920-1925 he pursued advanced studies in philosophy at Poznan and Lyon. In 1926 he was a member of the Polish mission in France (Lyon). In 1927, Cardinal Hlond, Primate of Poland, assigned him the spiritual ministration of Poles in Belgium, the Netherlands and Denmark. suburb of Paris, and later at Biarritz. From October 1940 to November, 1942, he was in Brazil attached to the Barnabite Fathers and Chaplain of the Notre-Dame de Lourdes Order as professor of Philosophy and Moral Theology.

Wheat Board Accounts
On the orders of the day:

I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Are the accounts of the Canadian wheat board audited by an officially appointed auditor? If so, who is the auditor and when will the last audit of the 1942-43 crop year be made available?
Order.

May I suggest to Your Honour, with great deference, that we are nearing the Easter recess and a number of matters such as the one raised by the member for Qu'Appelle have an urgency which otherwise they might not have. Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Before we go into interim supply there are one or two matters which I should like to bring up at this stage. If it is desirable to postpone my remarks, I have no objection to bringing the subject up later, but perhaps it might be just as well for me to proceed now.
In going into interim supply I realize that there is n,o necessity for any extended discussion of the resolution which the Acting Minister of Finance is about to introduce. Formal government requests of this kind have been granted time after time and we have no objec-

tion to that procedure being followed on this occasion. I take it the minister is asking for one-sixth of the regular civil estimates, including the supplementary estimates which were tabled the other day. The amount no doubt will be smaller than might appear from the total of the estimates themselves, since some of the estimates of the civil departments are statutory.
I hope the minister will be able to give to the house some plan or scheme being pursued as a policy by the government in connection with economies to be applied this year to civil estimates. We should like to know how they compare with last year's estimates. We want to know what is and what is not controllable. We want to know how the interest on the national debt, which, if my memory serves me correctly, was included last year in nonwar estimates, compares with the interest in the year before the war, and last year as well.
I would ask the minister at this stage to inform the house as to what plans are being laid down by the government in connection with a post-war taxation policy. That is one of the things we will need to know, so far as our committee is concerned. While economies are essential, and while we are anxious that not a cent will be wasted so far as non-war expenditures are concerned, at the same time I hope that consideration will be given to such matters as increase in old age pensions. We are hopeful that the age will be reduced, that the rate will be increased, and that due consideration will be given to the contributory feature mentioned in the speech from the throne.
The public accounts committee, which deals with matters relating to civil estimates, was set up at the beginning of the session. On February 25, the Prime Minister referred to that committee the public accounts and the auditor general's report. The committee has not yet met. I understand that one of the members of this party has already asked that the committee be convened. I suggest to the government that some other means ought to be made available under which, upon matters being submitted to them for consideration, this committee would automatically convene. I am hopeful that the committee on public accounts will begin its work, and that it will not be necessary on other occasions, as it was last year and has been again this year, to call attention to its failure to sit.
The public accounts committee has a big job on its hands. Many examinations are to be made. It is in that committee that the bulk of the work of examination of expenditures must be done. I refer, of course, to expenditures envisaged by the supply measure

Interim Supply Bill
now being introduced. I hope that the government will give some further latitude in respect of the type of material allowed to go before that committee. I remember that last year the public accounts committee was not allowed to deal with the wartime information board. That matter was referred to another committee and was not dealt with.
This party is anxious to facilitate the passage of interim supply. We reserve, however, our right to discuss any items in the various parts of supply as proceedings go on. I believe that is the undertaking which has always been given, and it is one I now ask the acting minister to give. May I caution the minister and the house that at a time like this members of the opposition and members generally must watch with ever-increasing care for waste and extravagance. For that reason we hope that when these estimates come down they will be in keeping with the general spirit of the times.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. McCann in the chair.

Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $46,331,283.90, being one-sixth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1945, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, be granted to His Majesty, on account, for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1945.
He said: The proposal this afternoon, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has said, has come to be a part of the regular course of financial procedure owing to the fact that the sittings extend considerably into the new fiscal year, making it impracticable to wait until the whole estimates are passed. The bill which will be founded on the resolution is to provide one-sixth of the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1944-45, which were tabled by the Minister of Finance on February 11, 1944, and which cannot be passed through all stages before the beginning of the new fiscal year, on Saturday, April 1. I think the leader of the opposition was in error when he suggested that this bill is one-sixth of the main estimates, plus the supplementary estimates. It is in fact one-sixth of the main estimates. The further supplementary estimates which were tabled the other day are supplementary with respect to the year 1943-44, and do not apply to the new fiscal year.
This is the usual proportion which is granted at the beginning of the year, and the amount asked is necessary not only to cover salaries and other normal costs of government for the first two months of the year,
but also to enable initial advances to outside offices, in order that their operations may be undertaken without delay. There are certain seasonal operations on which the heaviest expenditures occur in the early months of the year, and these have also to be financed. They include agricultural services, surveys and explorations, and sessional expenses of parliament, for which one-twelfth would be inadequate to provide for urgent requirements.
I want immediately to give to the house the undertaking mentioned by the leader of the opposition, namely that it is understood that the passing of this bill will- not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize and discuss any item in the estimates when they come up for discussion from time to time throughout the session. The usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of passing this measure.
My hon. friend has asked for certain things and, in what he has said, has dealt with two or three matters. As the committee will see, the total estimates this year amount to
8702,369,000.	This represents an increase of $54,455,000 over the appropriations for the current year 1943-44, which were $647,914,000. The committee will be interested in knowing how that increase was brought about. It is accounted for by additions to various expenditures which relate solely to the war or which result directly or indirectly from war conditions. The items are:
Increase of interest on public debt
and other debt charges	 $75,344,000
Increase in cost of administration of income tax and excess profits
tax	 1,199,000
Increase in post office service expenditures	 2,511,000

The first item answers the question asked by the leader of the opposition with regard to the increase in debt charges. This total will be compared with the net increase of this year's estimates over last year's of $54,455,000.
My hon. friend will not expect me this afternoon to go into details of possible economies. I am sure that these matters will be gone into fully when the estimates are being considered. In general, the policy of restricting normal peace-time expenditures to the minimum required for the maintenance of essential services is being continued. It is, however, considered necessary and desirable at this time to make provision for gradually intensifying certain scientific investigations and research as well as preparing the ground
Interim Sup-ply Bill

for the orderly expansion of our commercial and other relations at home and abroad. Preliminary steps along these lines are reflected in relevant appropriations throughout the estimates.
My hon. friend has indicated that there should be economy and paring of expenditures, but at the same time he has indicated that there should not be too many economies, that there are some items in connection with which he thinks increases should be made.
I just wanted common sense applied.

My hon. friend mentioned old age pensions. Old age pensions of course will be discussed at the appropriate time when whatever measure there is in that respect is brought down. I am not in a position this afternoon to make any announcement with respect to that. Neither am I in a position to accept my hon. friend's invitation to make an announcement with regard to the taxation policy. That is distinctly a budget announcement which will be made in due course.
I was dealing only with the post-war period.

My hon. friend asked what were the uncontrollable expenditures in these estimates. He brought that up, of course, because he realizes, as we' all do, that there are certain expenditures with respect to which economies, or at least paring, cannot be practised. The larger uncontrollable expenditures are as follows:
Interest on public debt and other
debt charges	 $307,058,000
European war pensions (1914-18).	37,000,000
Government contribution to unemployment insurance fund	 15,000,000
Old age pensions	 31,526,000
Other pensions and superannuation.	5,623,000
Care of returned soldiers (1914-18)	15,584,000
Subsidies and special compensation
to provinces	 98,876,000
Maritime Freight Rates Act		4,400,000
Sundry other items	 3,508,000

In the fiscal year 1938-39 interest on public debt and other debt charges required an expenditure of $133,147,000. The present estimates provide for an increase of over $174,000,000 in this item alone as compared with pre-war expenditures. I think that gives my hon. friend the comparisons he wanted. The first was a comparison of the debt charges of a year ago and those of to-day, and in this item the increase is roughly $75,000,000. The other was a comparison between the debt charges of 1938-39 and those of to-day, where the increase is about $174,000,000.

After deducting the total of uncontrollable items, namely $518,575,000, from the total of these estimates, there remains an amount of $183,794,000 from which reductions are theoretically possible. However, even in this sum are many services, such as those rendered to our primary industries, which it would be unwise to reduce even at this time.
I do not think my hon. friend will expect me to go into the matter of the public accounts committee. He knows and the committee knows that each committee is master of its own procedure. I vmderstand that it is in order, as soon as the committee is set up, for any member of it to give the clerk of the committee a notice which I believe the clerk acts upon and calls the committee together to give consideration to whatever business may be before it. He spoke also of enlarging-I think that was the word he used, or something to that effect-the scope of the committee or the type of reference which shall be made to the committee. In this respect I am not in position to say anything further than that the committee has the widest powers in respect to the examination of public accounts. The policy will be adopted which has been adopted in the past of giving the committee full scope in that respect.

I was not asking for any enlargement of the powers of the committee. I was asking only that the government accept the reference to the committee of such things as I referred to, such as the wartime information board, which was refused last year.

I am not familiar with the circumstances regarding the wartime information board. All I can say is that the committee has the right, subject to the usual rules of the house and to the rights of other committees, to consider any matter which is properly the subject of consideration by the public accounts committee and that those subjects are very broad. I do not think I have anything to add to this statement, unless there are some questions hon. members would like answered at this stage.

It was very difficult to hear the minister and I did not catch the figure he gave when he was dealing with uncontrollable expenditure. He referred to the interest on the funded debt, and I believe he mentioned $317,000,000.
The figure was $307,058,000.

On March 20, as reported on page 1668 of Hansard, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance gave the figure as of January 31, 1944,

Interim War Appropriation
as $268,312,935.81. Perhaps the figure the minister gave includes interest on the railway-debt.
Interest on public debt and other debt charges.
That would include interest on railway bonds?

speechtext: The figure of $26S,312,935.81 which I gave the other night represented the annual interest payable on the net funded debt as of January 31, 1944. As my hon. friend knows, it is going up all the time.
The minister is suggesting now that the figure of $307,000,000 is the estimate of what will be required for the coming fiscal year which will end March 31, 1945?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that a sum not exceeding $850,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or
under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending the thirty-first day of March, 1945, for the purposes and subject to the terms, conditions and limitations set out in the resolution on the orders of the day, to provide that sums not exceeding $3,650,000,000 be granted to His Majesty.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps at this stage, as at a similar stage of the previous resolution, I should say a word or two.
There should be no unnecessary delay in passing this interim war appropriation. A pretty full discussion has already taken place with respect to war departments and there will be an opportunity, of course, to discuss the other departments later; therefore I shall not discuss at any length the resolution now before us.
I would say to the minister, however, that for our protection we make the same reservation as to the position of the opposition so far as the rest of the war appropriation estimates are concerned, and I assume the minister is prepared to give the usual undertaking before this resolution passes.
The resolution deals entirely with matters pertaining to the war. Those in this country and in any others of the united nations engaged in this war who are apt to say in an unguarded moment that the war is nearing its end must now be ranked as real dangers themselves to the cause of the united nations. I am hopeful that this country yet will be aroused from its complacency with respect to the possibility of an early ending of hostilities. Our people have perhaps been depending too largely upon statements which have been made in other parts of the world because, while -we have passed the preparatory stages of the war, I think it may properly be said that we still have before us the most challenging and fiercest period of the war. This nation, this government, this parliament have to steel themselves not only against the great period of danger and peril which appears to lie immediately ahead, but against many blows, many losses, perhaps some reverses, before victory finally comes to our cause. I hope there will be an end of complacency among our people. Of necessity plans must be laid for the post-war period, and no one will object to a reasonable amount of legislation of that kind, but we must recognize that the first and the major issue which faces us is the winning of the war. To this end, subject to the right of criticism to ensure full prosecution of the war, this opposition is prepared, as it always has been, to give assistance in full measure to the government.
There are matters in this connection which the opposition cannot ignore if it is to discharge its duty. This leads me to bring to the

Interim War Appropriation

attention of the government, and more particularly to the minister who is piloting this resolution, some matters in connection with which remedial action is required in the interests of the preservation and maintenance of our democratic way of life. An answer which was given the other day to a question by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) shows that over 42,000 orders in council have been passed by this government since the war broke out. It stretches the imagination to accept the theory that every one of these orders was of the necessary and emergent type that the War Measures Act contemplates. There is a tendency on the part of governments, perhaps during peace, but especially in time of war, under the cloak of urgency, to pass legislation behind the closed doors of cabinet meetings without reference to the people as a whole. I hope the government will take into consideration the feeling which exists across this country in opposition to this movement which has gained so much impetus in the last few years, to legislate by orders in council rather than through parliament. Legislation by order in council is occasionally necessary; certainly there are times of national emergency when it is warranted. But there is an added responsibility upon the government to see to it that the people, when their representatives have not first been taken into consideration, are informed as to what that legislation is, and how the law is affected after the orders in council have been passed. That is not always done. Canadians will stand for this boardroom legislation or these semi-baked laws so long as it is necessary for the winning of the war, but if it oversteps that mark popular opinion will rebel against the usurpation of authority and power. One of our jobs as members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition is to draw to the attention of the government such abuses when they arise.
I shall take only a moment at this stage to give an illustration of board-room bureaucracy in operation. Yesterday's Globe and Mail reports a court case in Toronto, having to do with a question of permits for materials which are restricted during war time. Judge James Parker, who was trying the case, said he viewed the offence as a technical breach of a federal order in council, which, he noted, had precipitated a condition of confusion and of misunderstanding. Apparently the secretary of a company had read the Canada Gazette to find out whether the law permitted the company to make a certain purchase, and, not having found anything to prohibit it, they went ahead and made the purchase. A case was brought and came up on one or two occa-

sions. It was the subject of an application to the Supreme Court of Ontario, and Chief Justice Robertson, eminent jurist that he is, is reported as follows: He branded this as a very vicious principle, a tendency he noted in government orders in council of reversing a principle of justice and compelling people to come to court to prove their innocence. In this case the trial judge observed that there is confusion in all these orders in council. That is an example of the type of thing against which Canadians rebel when the opportunity is given them to voice their sentiments. I ask the minister and the government, in connection with war preparations, where things of this kind are normally likely to occur, to see to it that legislation by order in council and by war order shall be reduced to a minimum in the interest of the preservation of our democratic way of life.	.
Having criticized the government in this regard, I want to say a word or two with respect to another matter. In a few short weeks we shall be in the middle of a great campaign, the campaign for the sixth victory loan. Regardless of their views, political or other, the people of Canada can be counted upon to make a full and prompt response. We talk very lightly about equality of service, equality of sacrifice and equality of contribution. I often wonder if those of us who sometimes make these statements fully realize just what the terms actually mean to many of the Canadian people. When the sixth victory loan campaign is opened the Canadian people may well consider this: If everyone in Canada were to give, not just loan at interest, but every material thing we possessed, would anyone in Canada rise and say that that equalled the sacrifice, the service, and the contribution of the men and women who have given their lives or who are prepared to offer their lives upon the altar of sacrifice that we may have freedom, righteousness and liberty in the days that lie ahead?
With this plea to the people of Canada on the eve of the sixth victory loan I say that we ought to consider the position in which we find ourselves, which is one of safety and security, and compare and contrast it with what the No. 1 branch of our citizens overseas are now going through; we should then make up our minds as to what we shall do in connection with the lending of material things to help to see them through.
In conclusion I wish to say this to the government, as I said in a previous speech when the ordinary [DOT]estimates were before the house. We are prepared to give the government all the cooperation it deserves and needs

Interim War Appropriation
to win this war; but we reserve our right to criticize. That is in the interests of the government and in the interests of Canada as a whole. But I do think it means that our responsibility as a party, the government's responsibility, yes, the responsibility of those to the left of us and of all groups in Canada, is a very heavy one, calling for the greatest sacrifice and the greatest effort on the part of all of us.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Some time ago the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) placed an answer to some questions on Hansard. He said at that time that he was going to answer some other questions. He has not been back before the house since, and I thought I should take this opportunity of bringing the matter to the attention of the government and asking that the Minister of National Defence for Air make some statement before the house rises for the Easter recess.
The minister placed on Hansard at page 1401 an answer to a question by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) dealing with the. closing of certain airports across Canada. Some twenty-nine airports in Canada are to be closed. Since that answer was given there has been considerable discussion in the press, and I am sure that most members have been in receipt of a great many communications asking for further particulars. I think there are one or two things that ought to be stated by the government. It should be pointed out to the public just why the closing of these airports has suddenly been made necessary. Last fall-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Not suddenly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Last fall the
minister was making frantic appeals for aircrew. There was talk about the need for tremendous expansion of aircrew; that we were at the bottom of the barrel. We find now that there is a surplus of aircrew and that we do not need to train any more because we now have enough not only to take care of additional requirements but to take care of replacements in the event of losses. I know that the government of Canada cannot be fully responsible for that. This government is only a part of a great scheme being carried on by the British commonwealth of nations and the united nations; consequently they have to adjust their plans to the plans of the other members of the British commonwealth. Nevertheless, in fairness to the country generally, the minister ought to make a statement as to what changes in circumstances have brought about the need for 100-1241
closing these twenty-nine airports. He ought to make a statement to the house and to the country as to what basis was used in determining which airports would be closed. Was it on the basis of efficiency, or of proximity to points of embarkation?
In looking over the list I notice that eight airports are to be closed in Saskatchewan, eight in Ontario, eight in Alberta, two in Quebec, two in Manitoba and one in New Brunswick. It can be seen that most of the airports to be closed are in western Canada. Because our industrial facilities are extremely limited, the airports are about the only part of the war activity that has found its way on to the prairies. The closing of airports in eastern Canada would hardly work any economic hardship on the communities involved, because most of these communities are suffering from a lack of housing accommodation. But the closing of airports on the prairies will cause an economic readjustment in the communities involved. I am not complaining about that, because some time or other they have to be closed, and we shall all welcome the day when the war is over and we shall be able to turn the efforts and energies of this country to other purposes. But I do think it would help if the minister made some statement as to the basis used in deciding what airports should be closed and what airports should be kept open. It does seem to those of us who come from the west that it has thrown an unnecessarily heavy burden upon western Canada as compared with other parts of the country.
The government ought to make a statement very soon as to what could be done with the airports. In the town in which I live it will mean that some fifty or a hundred civilians will be thrown out of work. Rumours are going around to the effect that these airports may be reopened for vocational training; that the government will use them for the training of men who are being returned to civilian life. I would favour that. If the government plans to do that, however, the plans ought to be so dovetailed that when an airport is closed as a training centre it will be opened as soon afterwards as possible for the purposes of vocational training. If that were done the fifty or a hundred or more men affected would not be scattered all over the country looking for work. What is apt to happen if these airports are closed is that trained mechanics, electricians, carpenters and firemen will be allowed to move elsewhere looking for work, and then six or eight months-later an attempt will be made to assemble a group of trained men to maintain the airports. If they are to be used for some other-
Interim, War Appropriation

purpose, a liaison between the various departments, a dovetailing of their plans, could be arranged so that when an airport is closed for one purpose it can be kept ready to be opened for some other useful purpose. If the government finds that is not feasible, I hope plans are under way to move to some other centre the civilians employed in the airports to the end that their skill can still be made use of by the country in its war effort.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
I wish to make some inquiry of the Department of National Defence for Air with respect to , one of the airports that has been closed in my province. The minister is not in his seat, but his parliamentary assistant (Mr. Macmillan) is, and I therefore desire to direct my inquiry to him and to ask him if he can tell me why the Pennfield airport was closed and what is proposed to be done about it.
I am not quarrelling with the decision to close the airport.. I have no knowledge of the pros and cons of the question, but I would like to give something of the history of this airport. In the early stages of the war, when engineers from the Department of Transport were sent out to scout for probable airports in Canada, the location at Pennfield Ridge was indicated to them as being desirable for the establishment of an airport. I myself took some interest in the matter, because I was familiar with the terrain of the locality. When I found that there had been an adverse report from the engineer of the Department of Transport-I believe his name was McLean, if I remember rightly-I asked him and the deputy minister to come and see me in regard to the matter. They explained to me the conditions of the situation and the reasons which actuated them in making an adverse report upon this location. There were reasons of climatic conditions. Contiguity to the fogs of the bay of Fundy was alleged as a substantial reason why this airport should not be opened. After a good deal of doubt, after consulting with my friend, the member for Charlotte (Mr. Hill), who was more directly interested than I was from the standpoint of representation, I reluctantly came to the conclusion that possibly the report of the engineers was correct.
Imagine however my surprise when a few weeks later the announcement was made that an airport was to be established at Pennfield Ridge, that contracts were let to a contractor in New Brunswick on unit prices, without any competition, at a cost of millions. The history of that airport has been varied. At one time a navigation school was established there for men in the R.A.F.; then one day, coming from New Brunswick, I noticed on a siding alongside the train on which I was travelling a

special train loaded with airmen. I made inquiries and ascertained that the whole navigation school from Pennfield was being transferred to a point in the prairie provinces. That was no doubt done for good and sufficient reasons. Subsequently another school was set up there, largely composed, I believe, of personnel of the R.A.F. I am not sure whether there were any of the R.C.A.F. men there, or what the position was. That school has now been closed down but-and this is the point of the remarks I desire to make- just previous to the closing down of the school, I am informed, a contract was let to a contractor without any tenders being called for, on unit prices, which would double the surface areas of the runway, at a cost of half a million dollars. The school is closed and no announcement has been made as to the purpose of this installation, which now must have cost more than 83,000,000. That is a guess on my part. I have no figures available, but judging from, what has been done and what I know of the area and the extent of the installation, there cannot have been much less than $3,000,000 spent on that airport. And the work is going on. This half million expenditure has not been suspended. I think some explanation is due to the public and the country.

Does my hon. friend
know-

speechtext:

I come now to the third matter mentioned by the leader of the opposition, which had to do with the text that the war is not yet won. I agree with him, and I have endeavoured to preach as serious sermons as I possibly could along those same lines. When the Minister of Finance introduced this measure in the first place he referred to the same subject, as reported on page 391 of Hansard, as follows:
I need not assure the house that this probable reduction in direct war expenditures, like the corresponding decrease forecast by President Roosevelt in connection with United States war expenditures, does not represent any slackening in the war effort, but rather merely the result of the stage of the war and of our preparation for war which has now been reached. The speech from the throne clearly indicated that while the war situation has improved from the point of view of the united nations during the past year, nevertheless the duty of the government is to see that Canada's war effort is firmly maintained until the enemy is defeated in Europe and in Asia. The winning of the war clearly remains the first of all our objectives.
I agree thoroughly with my hon. friend. Too many people are thinking that the war is won, but all they need to do is to ask the men who are in front of Cassino, the men who are on the Anzio beachhead, the men who are on the right flank near Ortona, the men who are in the air flying over Germany and Europe, many of them not coming back, the men who are risking their lives ploughing the seas to protect our men and munitions in transit. All they need to do is to look back at the same period in the last war. They will realize that the situation is not the same. The German is far from beaten; he does not consider he is beaten and he fights on. The Jap is quite willing to die as he always has been in order to maintain his place in the sun. Progress in Italy has been quite gratifying, but we are still 800 or 900 miles from Germany, and there is a long hard road ahead of us in the south of Europe. On the north we find that at the same period in the last war we were in control of probably three-quarters of France, but to-day we have not even a toe-hold on the north west coast of Europe. The whole of Europe still has to be regained.
We pay tribute to our gallant allies the Russians. The fighting of the Russians will probably have to be matched this year. In the far east China is overrun. Hong Kong must be avenged, and Singapore, the Malaya peninsula, the Philippines and those islands in the southwest Pacific must be retaken. That is what we must do before we finally bring our enemies to unconditional surrender. That is quite a task. I refer those who think the war is nearly won to the statement made a day or two ago by the director of aircraft production, that by this time next year we may quite possibly have to be building planes just as hard as we are to-day. Let us hope that that will not be so.
I agree wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Weyburn when he says that we will welcome the day when the war is over and we can turn our energies toward the constructive work of peace. I am glad to hear that
Interim. War Appropriation

declaration made. We hear complaints when this or that activity is not being kept up. One would almost think that some people wanted the war to continue in order that certain war activities might be kept going. What we want is to end the war just as soon as possible. The sooner we can get it over, the sooner we can relax our efforts. However, the more we intensify our efforts at this time, the shorter will be the war and the quicker and surer the victory that is to come.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury referred to a particular airport. Without accusing him of unfairness, I think he need not have brought that up this afternoon. The Minister of National Defence for Air is not in the house at present. I am sure my hon. friend knew of the circumstances to which he has referred when the estimates of the Minister of National Defence for Air were before the committee. That was the time to have brought them up. I can say to my hon. friend that a statement will be made in due course with regard to that matter. I say to the hon. member for Weyburn that a statement will be made in due course with regard to the matter of closing airports.
I do not know whether any statement can be made as to the method adopted to establish what particular airport will be closed and what particular airport will be kept open, but if any statement can be made I am sure it will be made when the time comes. The hon. member inquired as to what would be done with the aii-ports when they are closed. I am sure that that matter was discussed by my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air, when his appropriations were being considered and I assume that there will be an opportunity for further discussion before the session is over.

speechtext: I do not quite understand the attitude taken this afternoon by the minister. It seems that every time a matter is brought before the house the opposition is criticized for endeavouring to have it elucidated.

speechtext:
We take second place to no one in our desire for the mobilization of this nation for victory, but we seem to be always met with criticism, either direct or veiled, when we bring up matters. The attitude taken is that we should be shoved aside, that when we offer criticism, whether it is constructive or not, we do so for some ulterior purpose. I thought I would see what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said during the last war about the attitude of the opposition. I think his words summarize and epitomize the attitude that should characterize us all in endeavouring to assist the government when it needs assistance. This is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said on March 10, 1915, as reported on page 834 of Hansard:
... it was never intended by me nor by any of those who sit around me that, when we wei;e summoned to parliament and called upon to pass judgment, to sanction or not to sanction the measures brought down by the government, we were to abdicate our judgment and to sit here as recording machines, simply to register the decisions of the government.
I re-echo those words. Sir Wilfrid Laurier has epitomized the attitude of the opposition in tvar time. He continued:
We are still of the opinion that the war is the supreme issue-
That attitude is the attitude to-day of those in opposition.
-but if we believe that in the method of carrying on the war, in the policy proposed by the government, there be errors of judgment or otherwise, then it is our imperative, duty to cry halt, to show the mistakes, to point out the true course and to use every endeavour to prevent mistakes from being carried into effect.
That is the attitude of this opposition. There has been altogether too much of an attitude on the part of the government of castigating members of the opposition when we, with the same desire as the government to assist in the winning of the war, bring forward what we believe to be constructive criticism.

What is happening here is this. We have had before us for some time the main war appropriation resolution. Every member has had and will have the opportunity of discussing with the minister interested any item in his estimates. After that is done the resolution is passed. Then we go into committee on the bill, and once more hon. members of the house have the fullest opportunity, if they so desire, to discuss every item of war expenditure in every department that is affected. Has that right been taken away by what we are doing this afternoon? Not in the slightest. But because we need a portion of the money to make urgently needed immediate payments the hon. member for Lake Centre would suggest that some right is taken away from him. He has all the rights I have mentioned. He has his opportunity to discuss every one of the items of, the war appropriation on the main resolution itself and again when the war appropriation bill is before the house.
But because he cannot have two more opportunities to discuss these items he comf plains that we are taking away the rights of an opposition which were asserted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. My hon. friend has a vivid imagination. I repeat that all he is doing is to set up a straw man in order to knock him down again. The opposition still has its full right to criticize any item of the war appropriation, but I thought there was a general understanding that in order that we might get along with the business of the country and the prosecution of the war $850,000,000 out of a total war appropriation of $3,650,000,000 should be granted now so that we could make immediate payments, reserving full rights to the whole house to discuss everything. I say to my hon. friend that I do not think Sir Wilfrid Laurier whose statements he has quoted would ask for anything more than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
In spite of what the minister has just said, I still think we are entitled to a statement from the Minister of National Defence for Air or his parliamentary assistant, and it seems to me that when this interim appropriation is being granted the minister for air should at least be here.
In 1943 airports were being erected in different parts of Canada. The province of Manitoba had one at Gimli. The cost of these airports runs into millions of dollars. The minister for air stated in the house on February 29 that some of the airports would be closed, but he did not indicate how many. On March 13, it was announced that twenty-eight airports were to be closed. If there has been a sudden reversal of policy in the matter of airports ye should be told about it. There was a conference held at Quebec last August and September which cost this country $366,000. What was the policy then laid down with regard to airports? At that time the minister was still asking for an expansion of the air training programme and he continued to do so until November of that year. This year there was a sudden reversal of policy and it was announced in February that twenty-eight airports were to be closed this year. The people of Canada are asking the reason for this sudden change of policy, and I think they are entitled to an answer. The Canadian people have questioned very little the expending of money to be used in the winning of this war, but they certainly are critical of what appears to them to be unnecessary waste, and I think a statement is due from the minister to the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
I wish to bring a matter of some little urgency to the attention of the

Interim War Appropriation

minister. It will take only a minute or two. I promise that I am not going to be critical; rather I want to be helpful. I would not have brought the matter up to-day except that in view of the Easter recess and our adjourning this week I presume there will not be another opportunity for me to do so.
In the war appropriation estimates of the Minister of Agriculture there is an item, "Subsidies to producers of food products," for a considerable sum. So far the subsidies have been paid over the last two or three years but I am sorry to say that I now have complaints that these subsidies are very much in arrears, somewhat to the embarrassment of the processors of milk, butter and other food products. I would ask the minister to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture with a view to seeing that the subsidies are brought up to date. I am not blaming the officials of the department in any way because I know they are capable, and it is undoubtedly true that complicated calculations have to be made and a good deal of time is required for scrutiny of the accounts. Without further delay, and not to hold up the war appropriation I would ask the minister to see if something cannot be done to ensure that the subsidies are brought up to date.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY -INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence a matter of serious concern to Saskatchewan and one over which he has supervision. I assume that some of the money which is now being appropriated will be used to further the plan already well under way. There is an extensive military establishment at the town of Maple Creek, Saskatchewan, where a basic training centre has been established. That is now virtually closed. There are only enough men left in that centre to look after it. Then we have that great thriving centre, in the northern part of the province, the city of Prince Albert, where there are splendid barracks and other accommodation, used last winter for experimental purposes. The only ones left there now are a few men to guard the place. Complaints are now coming in to me that the military camp at Dundum is fast dwindling in importance and that units will shortly be moved from that centre. To cap. the climax of a woeful tale, the great metropolitan centre, the queen city of the west, Regina, is fast dwindling in military importance.

maintopic: LOAN OF $1,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the parliamentary assistant to the minister with regard to this section. What is the method of financing this particular transaction of $1,000,000,000? The section authorizes the loan. In what form is the loan to be? It is under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act and, as I understand it, some of it is permanent finance authorized in the resolution and consists of the sale of bonds and other securities. Some of it is temporary and refunding finance. Is that not true? Is not some of it to be in the form of treasury notes? We are talking about a billion dollars. The function of an opposition is to find out something about it. The resolution and all of that is all right, but when the bill is before parliament, which binds future generations yet unborn to pay back the loan, it is the duty of the opposition to find out something about the method and manner of financing.
In addition to that, I should like to know what kind of audit we have. As I understand it under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit
Government Loan

Act the auditor general cannot do a thing about this billion dollars. The parliamentary assistant to the minister, if he had been in the house in the last two years when the minister was asked these questions, would have found out that since the war started there has been substituted for the auditor general who audits the revenues and expenditures of the country, and has done so since confederation, a comptroller of the treasury. As long as the comptroller of the treasury finds that any item in this particular billion dollar loan is within the four corners of the resolution on war appropriation expenditure which has been adopted, he has to pass it. As was said by the hon. member for Temiscouata in the last two sessions-and I agreed with him-the comptroller of the treasury is more or less an official of the Minister of Finance. He is appointed by the minister and is under his control. Under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act he has not the power which the auditor general used to have in days of peace.
What is the practice with regard to financing? Once upon a time we used to borrow money through the medium of treasury notes. In the last war we got money at the lowest of costs, less than one per cent on treasury notes, from Chase's bank and the National City bank of New York. We borrowed large sums of money at a time when the provinces and the municipalities were in the market and they could not borrow in any shape or form without the consent of the Minister of Finance of Canada. That may or may not have been a good policy. In some respects it was no doubt a good policy; but at the same time I wish to point out what was said at that time. We borrowed money on treasury notes and refunded at a loss. I think it was the present Minister of Finance who preceded the present minister who said that we borrowed money at the rate of less than one per cent. It was in the form of treasury notes and other negotiable instruments. We are in the fifth year of the war and we have a new victory loan coming on. I say that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance should, before Easter, make a further statement with regard to the resolution which preceded this bill and the coming victory loan. No doubt a part of it will be taken care of by the billion dollars and other matters in the coming fiscal year.
All these victory loans have cost us too much. The method of financing has cost us too much. The public is being charged too much and future generations are being charged too much. The interest rate is too high, and there are a great many unnecessary expenditures incurred in connection with these loans. They will have to be met out of section 2 of fMr. Church.]
this bill which authorizes short term loans and long term loans. Before the Easter recess the finance department should issue a statement in connection with the loan and the matters to which I have referred to-day, because in my opinion this large expenditure of a billion dollars is costing Canada too much. We should have a lower rate of interest, one or one and one-half per cent. No doubt some of the money will come from the Bank of Canada and the chartered and affiliated banks. Some of it may be a straight loan. No doubt different methods will be adopted. In the fifth year of the war I think we can get money at a far less rate of interest than we are paying up to date. Future generations will have to pay for this war. In my opinion a great part of the expenditures which are the basis of this loan is not for war at all. If we go over the various bills which are passed here and if we examine the appropriation bill of one billion 1 dollars we shall find a great many items in them that have nothing to do with war. Wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen at the scene of combat, not at home. You do not win wars by a whole lot of expenditure at home on matters that will not do very much to win wars.
What is Mr. Morgenthau, the treasurer of the United States, doing? Recently he took a trip to Italy. While there, he met soldiers and when he came back he told a committee of congress that the soldiers were objecting to suffering in flesh and blood in this war and then being asked to pay for the war when they came home. I think the time has come to put the brakes on the high rate of interest that is being charged and other extravagant costs of loans.
The large standing national committees across Canada are spending money like water in many unnecessary ways.
The parliamentary assistant may smile at this kind of thing, but I can point out to him instances where money has been wasted in connection with loans. I have seen wooden platforms, which the newspapers said cost $10,000, erected for the purposes of parades, speeches, actresses who have been brought from the United States-and that during this strenuous period of the war. More than that, expenditures have been incurred for transportation, staterooms, meals, luncheons, hotel bills, and many other things which the war expenditures committee long ago should have stopped. I do not wish to criticize the national committee; far from it. But I do say that these are expenditures that should be investigated. I have spoken to many business men, some of them connected with

Government Loan
banks and others representing large taxpayers in the city I come from, and this is their view.
I- am not one of those who are eager to criticize the loan; not at all. But there are a great many people who are suggesting that the time has come now to cut out the frills, because we are in the fifth year of the war, and it should not be necessai-y for us to go to Hollywood to get actors and actresses to help us to sell bonds to the Canadian people. I do hope that the loan will be a great success. That hope is shared by everyone else. I repeat, however, that the time has come for us to cut down materially on these unnecessary expenditures. That sort of thing may have been all right in the first two or three years of the war, but the- Canadian people realize now that the winning of the war is the main thing. That is our sole objective at the moment. Nothing else matters. There will be no financing of anything, and life itself will be unbearable, if we do not win the war. All domestic matters, however important they may be, must be subordinated to this end. They can wait.
I suggest to the acting minister that some new and more modern method of financing ought to be announced, and it should be an improvement on some of the practices that we have followed in the past. I would point out that this is a changing war. As I say, we are in the fifth year of the war and changes are being made from week to week, from month to month, in machines in the air, on land and on the sea, and in connection with equipment and supplies of various kinds. Many things which were perfectly legitimate, many things which were in every way modern and efficient but a short time ago, have been rendered obsolete by research and scientific investigation generally in this changing war.
I see the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), is here, and I appeal to him, as I do to every other member of the house, to urge upon the government the importance of giving to the public, before the first day of the victory loan campaign, a comprehensive statement along the lines I have indicated from someone in the finance department. I. am not saying all this merely to indulge in destructive criticism. I would not have said anything but for the fact that myself I have noticed some of the things I have pointed out. I may say, I noticed some of it in the last war also. My object is to see if we cannot effect some economies.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The resolution provides for the refunding of matured, maturing and callable financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways and for the issue of securities guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada in respect of such refunding, to an aggregate principal amount not exceeding 8200,000,000. The volume of business of the railroads during this war in terms of trains, coaches, rolling stock, freight, ocean, and land services such as hotels, is sky-high as compared with the volume of business in the last war. The railroads of Canada and the United States have been making considerable money out of this war. A pamphlet was issued by the national city bank of New York, which has large investments in United States and Canadian railroads, outlining the comparison in traffic in the two wars and the methods of financing.
A return was made to the house last session showing the earnings of the two railroad systems during the present war. Up to the close of 1940, the first fifteen months of the war, the Canadian National Railways, a public utility, had made 82,500,000, and I believe the earnings of the other railroad were about $2,750,000. These railroads have made more in fifteen or sixteen months of this war than they did during the whole of the last war.
Some of these securities should have been retired out of earnings. Why should we pyramid interest and principal sky-high and not pay something off? The earnings are so large that they could easily have paid off half of these maturing and callable financial obligations. The day of payment is being postponed and the interest debt for generations yet unborn will be fabulous.
We have the committee on railways and shipping which used to be set up by means of a resolution. However, at the last session and the session before, the committee was appointed simply by not giving notice in votes and proceedings. It is now a standing committee and no resolution needs to be passed by the house. When a resolution was presented there was an opportunity for debate and the company had to put their cards on the table. Now all we know about it is a resolution like this one, to pay in the future. If it is passed a report will come in the dying days of the session from this useless select committee. I doubt whether any of the reports were concurred in last session.
Some of the obligations herein were incurred during the days when the company had very big eyes, when they were building branch lines and duplicating hotel and other ocean and land services without any hope of ever being able to pay the fixed charges. Ontario is the forgotten province as far as rolling stock and
other matters are concerned. Some of the subsidiaries which operate in the United States have the best of rolling stock and equipment, but all Ontario gets are the old rattle-box cars with which to move troops and civilians. The troops, as soldiers, should be given cut rates, but this public utility and government railway is charging very high rates. No weekend rates for soldiers are given even in the Toronto district or in the district represented by you, Mr. Chairman.
This is not the kind of government financing we should have in the fifth year of the war. Part of these obligations should be paid out of earnings. I doubt whether there is sufficient security for many of the subsidiaries of this company. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) is familiar with one subsidiary of this railway. There are two old boats running between Toronto and Port Dalhousie. Fifteen or twenty years ago one of these boats was not considered good enough to run between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. But it is dumped down in Toronto and is now considered good enough for Ontario.
The members who represent Ontario do not act as a unit like the maritime members and those who come from the Pacific coast or the prairies. Ontario has to put up with these things because nothing is said here about them. There is no doubt that the railroads have made a magnificent and glorious showing in this war. The load in passengers and freight they have been carrying constitutes a marvellous record. I submit that the railways and shipping committee should be asked to make a report on this particular matter because if they are going to function, they should function properly.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) was absolutely right when he suggested that the auditors' report should be referred to the committee. Parliament appoints the auditors and they are supposed to be responsible to parliament, but we never see the audit. How many members of this House of Commons have seen it? I know I have never seen it. This committee should be set up the first or second day of the session. This railroad has been making tremendous earnings and it should be giving some of them back to the people who will have to pay this debt. Some relief should be given from the high rates that are being charged, especially at week-ends. There should be relief granted in freight rates also. Our soldiers and civilians should not have to ride in the rattle-boxes in which they often are forced to ride while United States subsidiary lines, on which a large sum of money has been spent by this

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, March 24, consideration in committee of bill No. 35, to amend the Exchequer Court Act-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. McCann in the chair.
On section 2-Power to appoint a deputy judge.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
I should like to know from the Minister of Justice whether the only change is the adding of another judge to the court?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
I think another judge is necessary. We all know that after the last war a large number of contracts were involved in proceedings before the court, and many years elapsed before they were all settled. The government has announced a new policy by which a certain percentage is paid-I suggest fifty per cent; in the United States, I believe it is sixty per cent, which will mean a great deal more work for the court. As I understand it, this court is excluded from the provincial field as regards royal commissions appointed by provincial attorneys general under the Inquiries Act, which is both federal and provincial in its application, and these judges will not be liable for commission duty, whether federal or provincial.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have not looked at the exact terms of the statute, but I do not know of any case of a judge of the exchequer court having been requested to act as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act; and no change is being made by this bill. But I should need to look at the terms to see
whether the president and a puisne judge of the exchequer court would be competent to be called. I know of no case in my experience at the bar where it has happened.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
It seems to me that in view of the work which the exchequer court is doing, and which is largely financial, business and commercial, there should be a much higher scale of fees. The revenues of the court should be very considerable in view of the magnitude of the contracts and other business involved, and so far as I know they have not been raised, at any rate very much, since the last war. Surely the country should not have to pay the whole of the bill for a court like this. In my opinion it should be self-sustaining.
Mr. ST. LAURENT. A great many cases which come before the exchequer court are claims by the subject against the crown, and I do not know that it would be proper to increase the scale of fees which the subject would be called upon to provide when making a claim against the crown. There are other fields of jurisdiction where, perhaps, the suggestion of the hon. member could very well be considered, and I should be glad to take it up with the officers of my department. But I should not like to give the impression that there is any intention of increasing the cost to the subject when prosecuting a claim against the crown.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
The services of exchequer court judges have been used on occasion on royal commissions, have they not? As a matter of fact, they have been used on provincial royal commissions as well as federal royal commissions. I thought, in view of the statement made by the minister, there might be some misunderstanding in that connection. I have here a return, No. 182 of 1941, dealing with the question of royal commissions, a matter which I brought up the other evening. From 1923 to the date of the return there were, I believe, eighty-one royal commissions set up upon which judges have sat, and some very large fees have been paid to judges in this connection in addition to their salaries. In one case the fees during the period amounted to over S40,000, and in one or more other cases exceptionally large fees or allowances have been paid. So far as the exchequer court is concerned, at least two commissions- one under the Department of Fisheries, another Under the Department of Labour- were presided over by a judge of the exchequer court. I think, having regard to the fact that there is such a considerable body of work to be done by judges, they should not
Exchequer Court Act

be utilized in connection with royal commissions. According to the last figures available the number of judges in Canada is 278. Some of them are sitting on government boards, others on commissions and the like. I again bring to the attention of the minister the need of making a provision that, in the interests of their own independence, if for no other reason, judges should not be allowed to accept extra allowances by occupying positions on royal commissions. This is a practice which is productive of considerable criticism. The other night mention was made of a situation in the province of Saskatchewan. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to making provision that the judiciary shall be used exclusively as a judiciary and that its services shall not be used in connection with commissions, particularly those involving political considerations of any kind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
No. It is six o'clock and I do not see any reason why we should go on. Would the minister entertain an amendment to this bill along the lines I suggested the other evening? It seems to mo, if another judge is required in the exchequer court, because of the extra business during the war and in the immediate postwar period, that a time limit should be set. An appointment could be made for, let us say, three or five years, and if at the end of that time it were found that there was still sufficient work to warrant another judge in the exchequer court a bill could be passed by the house for another period. What we are doing now is creating a position in perpetuity. If, after the war, we should come to a time when there would be a small amount of work in this court we shall still have this position, and it is very unlikely that we shall reduce the size of the exchequer court to what it was in the days before the war when we had only two judges. Would the minister consider that suggestion before the legislation is finally passed?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should not like to undertake to find a judge who would accept an appointment to the exchequer court for any period such as the hon. member mentions. The experience of the last several years has shown that there is more war work there than the two judges of the court can perform as expeditiously as those who have to come before the court would like to see generally; and it has been felt that it would be in the public interest to provide an additional judge in that court. I do not think it would be
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
possible to do so if the legislation were to have a limitation as to time. I do not. think the House of Commons would be well advised to try to determine at this time what should be done a few years hence. I kiiow it is always difficult to reduce the complement of a court; but should a situation arise in the future when Canadian citizens and those having claims against the crown or those against whom the crown has claims felt they no longer required a court to deal with such matters, the matter might properly be brought up, but I should not like to put a limitation upon a bill of this kind, if as is generally recognized there is requirement for an additional judge.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.
